content: Latin is an ancient Indo-European language that was spoken during the Roman Republic and Roman Empire. The expansion of Roman conquests spread the language across the Mediterranean and much of Europe. Latin existed in two primary forms: Classical Latin, which was used in formal prose and poetry, and Vulgar Latin, which was the spoken language of the common people. After the fall of the Roman Empire, Latin became the universal language of the Roman Catholic Church and the lingua franca of educated Europeans. Although its widespread use began to decline in the 1600s, Vulgar Latin evolved into regional dialects, which eventually developed into the modern Romance languages. English, despite being a Germanic language, has borrowed approximately 35% of its vocabulary from Latin, primarily through French but also directly, especially during the 1600s. Latin remains influential in fields such as science, law, and academia. Ecclesiastical Latin continues to be used in the Roman Catholic Church, and Classical Latin is still taught in schools, often alongside Greek in the study of Classics. The Latin alphabet, derived from the Old Italic alphabet and ultimately from the Greek alphabet, is the most widely used writing system in the world today. Latin originated as a member of the Italic language family and was brought to the Italian peninsula by the Latins in the 9th or 8th century BCE. It developed in Latium, near the Tiber River, where Roman civilization emerged. Early Latin was influenced by the Etruscan language, a non-Indo-European language spoken in northern Italy. While Classical Latin is the form preserved in Roman literature, the spoken language of the Western Roman Empire was Vulgar Latin, which differed significantly in grammar, vocabulary, and pronunciation. Although Latin was the official language of the Roman Empire, Greek became the dominant language of the educated elite, as much of the literature and philosophy studied by Romans originated from Greek authors. In the Eastern Roman Empire, which later became the Byzantine Empire, Greek eventually replaced Latin as the legal and governmental language. The Latin alphabet, as used by the Romans, lacked punctuation, letter spacing, and lowercase letters. For example, the phrase Philosophia est ars vitae (Philosophy is the art of life) would have been written as PHILOSOPHIAESTARSVITAE. The modern Latin alphabet has been adapted for use in many languages, including Romance, Celtic, Slavic, and Germanic languages. The spread of the Roman Empire facilitated the dissemination of Latin throughout Europe. Over time, Vulgar Latin diverged into distinct regional dialects, which became the Romance languages by the 9th century. Initially, these languages were primarily spoken, while Latin remained the language of writing. For instance, Latin was the official language of Portugal until 1296, when it was replaced by Portuguese. Among the Romance languages, Italian is considered the closest to Latin in terms of vocabulary, while Sardinian is the most conservative in terms of phonology. Differences between Classical Latin and the Romance languages, such as the loss of case endings and changes in stress patterns, have been used to reconstruct Vulgar Latin. Romanian retains some case distinctions, but these are thought to be influenced by the Balkan linguistic area. Latin has also had a significant impact on English, particularly through ecclesiastical usage during the medieval period and through the Anglo-Norman language after the Norman Conquest. From the 16th to the 18th centuries, English writers created numerous new words from Latin and Greek roots, some of which, like imbibe and extrapolate, remain in use today. Many common polysyllabic English words are derived from Latin, often through Old French. Latin mottos and phrases are still widely used by organizations. Latin is a synthetic, fusional language, meaning that it uses affixes attached to fixed stems to express grammatical categories such as gender, number, and case in nouns, pronouns, and adjectives (a process called declension) and person, number, tense, voice, mood, and aspect in verbs (a process called conjugation). Latin nouns are categorized into five declensions, each with specific endings for cases such as nominative (subject), genitive (possession), dative (indirect object), accusative (direct object), ablative (separation or instrument), and vocative (direct address). Latin verbs are grouped into four conjugations based on their infinitive endings (-āre, -ēre, -ere, -īre) and are described by four principal parts, which provide the forms needed to conjugate the verb in all tenses, moods, and voices. Latin instruction in schools and universities typically focuses on reading and translating texts rather than speaking or listening. However, the Living Latin movement advocates for teaching Latin as a spoken and written language, similar to modern languages. This approach aims to provide a deeper understanding of Latin literature and poetry by emphasizing the sounds and rhythms of the language. Institutions such as the Vatican and the University of Kentucky offer programs in Living Latin, and organizations like the National Junior Classical League promote the study of Latin among students. Modern Latin is still used in specialized fields such as philosophy, medicine, and law, where terms like subpoena duces tecum and q.i.d. (quater in die, meaning four times a day) remain in use. Latin has also been employed in films set in the Roman Empire, such as Sebastiane and The Passion of the Christ. Additionally, Latin translations of modern literature, including Harry Potter and The Lord of the Rings, aim to sustain interest in the language. The Pope continues to deliver official messages in Latin, underscoring its enduring role in the Roman Catholic Church.
